checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: 1B URLs, and short codes must never collide. Which generator?

options.label: Hash + base62
options.verdict: Deterministic, so the same long URL always yields the same code and you get dedup for free. But truncating a hash reintroduces birthday collisions, so every write still has to check the table before it can commit.

options.label: Counter + base62
options.verdict: Unique by construction — no collision check on the write path at all. Sequential codes are guessable, which you fix by XOR-ing the counter with a 64-bit secret before encoding: still unique, no longer enumerable.

defend.prompt: Defend it. What does the counter actually cost you?

options.label: Codes are enumerable unless you obfuscate them
It cannot dedup two submissions of the same URL
The counter is a coordination point that must not be lost
Codes grow past 8 characters within the first billion

defend.explain: 62^7 already covers 3.5 trillion codes, so length is not the worry. The real costs are enumeration, loss of dedup, and turning the counter into a piece of state you must never roll backwards.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder
checkpoints.prompt: 100M DAU, 5 redirects each. What does the read path have to survive?

rungs.note: 500M / 86,400s. Round the day to 100k seconds and it falls out as 5k.
~600k RPS. This is the number the read path is actually designed against, not the average.

checkpoints.explain: Writes are ~1/sec against ~600k/sec of reads: a 1000:1 ratio. Every later decision — cache, CDN, replicas — is a consequence of that one number.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the redirect path so a hot short code never touches disk.
checkpoints.explain: A 302 from the CDN edge serves the hottest codes without ever reaching your origin. Behind it, the read service checks Redis first; Postgres is the miss path only. Write service and Redis counter belong to the create path, and Elasticsearch is not in this story at all.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: p99 redirect latency just went from 40ms to 900ms.
checkpoints.explain: Postgres is the loudest number, but it is the symptom. The cache hit rate fell 34 points, so roughly a third of reads that used to be served from memory are now queued behind disk. Fix Postgres and you have treated the burn; fix the eviction or key churn that collapsed the hit rate and the 900ms disappears.

wrong.Postgres primary: That is where the latency shows up, but ask why it is suddenly receiving traffic it never used to see.
wrong.Read service: +12ms is it waiting on something downstream, not the cause.
wrong.CDN edge: A single point of hit rate does not explain a 22x latency change.
